items.content:
Every quarter at Sierra, we celebrate the end of the quarter with Double Denim Day (or, as some like to call it, Canadian Tuxedo Day) 👖. This Q3, we needed a lot of denim to celebrate the most remarkable quarter in Sierra's 2.5 year history.

We added over $150M ARR this quarter, bringing our total ARR beyond $400M. Remarkably, we added more ARR in one quarter than we had all of last year.

The most exciting thing to me is that our pace is accelerating. It took us six months to double from $100M to $200M ARR, and only five months to double from $200M to $400M ARR.

@claybavor and I are grateful to our customers and proud of the entire Sierra team.

items.title:
People are celebrating how much time they're saving by letting agents review their code.

But be hon...
items.content:
People are celebrating how much time they're saving by letting agents review their code.

But be honest: how much time are you spending fixing bugs afterward?

Saving two hours on code review means nothing if you then spend four hours fixing problems.

If you really want to know whether your automated code reviews are saving you time, you gotta measure the whole thing:

1. Track how much time you spend reviewing code, including the agent's feedback.

2. Track how much time you spend fixing bugs that make it past review.

3. Track how much time you spend investigating incidents and dealing with affected customers.

Compare the total time with what it took before introducing agentic reviews. Ideally, measure it per PR or per change so you're comparing similar workloads.

At the end of the day, nobody cares how much time you are saving on a particular task.

The ultimate goal is to save more time overall without deploying crap to production.
items.author: @svpino
items.summary: svpino argues that celebrating time saved by AI agent code reviews is misleading unless teams measure end-to-end: time spent on reviews, fixing bugs that slip past review, and handling production incidents. He proposes tracking total time per PR and comparing against pre-agent baselines, emphasizing overall time savings and quality over per-task savings.

items.title: Edison Scientific CEO @SGRodriques reveals how an AI agent discovered a potential treatment for blin...
items.content:
Edison Scientific CEO @SGRodriques reveals how an AI agent discovered a potential treatment for blindness:

"We published in Nature about an agent called Robin, the first agent I believe anyone developed that could propose experiments, get data, update the experiments, and make a new discovery."

"By combing through tens of thousands of hypotheses, Robin identified how an existing class of drugs, Rho-kinase inhibitors, could treat dry age-related macular degeneration, a major cause of blindness."

"That did not appear anywhere in the scientific literature. We tested it in mice and got positive results."

"That was early 2025. Since we made Kosmos, something like 20,000 or 50,000 novel scientific findings have been generated for our partners, one of which is Pfizer."

He adds that their newer Kosmos system has generated tens of thousands of novel findings for partners including Pfizer.
items.reasoning: Substantive first-person account of an AI-driven scientific discovery with real-world validation (Nature publication, mouse results, pharma partnerships). High technical and societal relevance for AI in drug discovery, though engagement is modest and the underlying work dates to early 2025, so it is retrospective rather than breaking news.

items.title: Epoch AI researcher @AlexBarry4 reveals how AI can turn a company's own security fixes into working ...
items.content:
Epoch AI researcher @AlexBarry4 reveals how AI can turn a company's own security fixes into working exploits before users even get the update:

"We got GLM 5.3 to go look for security fixes that Mozilla had already made to Firefox in their development repo, but that hadn’t made it to the stable release yet."

"Mozilla and many other companies are using frontier LLMs to scan their code base and patch vulnerabilities."

"That's valuable work. But if you don't also ensure those get pushed to users as quickly as possible, you’re saying, hey, for the next one week or four weeks, here’s a vulnerability in our software."

"Models are getting increasingly good at decompiling binaries. It's not implausible that open weight models can take the old binary and the new binary, figure out which bit corresponds to a security patch, and reverse engineer an attack."
@EpochAIResearch

items.title:
How do you make a chip design agent more reliable and efficient?

The @Siemens EDA team used NVIDIA ...
items.content:
How do you make a chip design agent more reliable and efficient?

The @Siemens EDA team used NVIDIA NeMo Gym to check the engineering files its agent produced, trace errors, and improve the agent’s skills and tool descriptions.

In its standard cell characterization benchmark, those changes raised the composite verification score from ~55% to ~95%, with 66% fewer agent turns and 64% fewer output tokens.

We just published a new techblog that walks through what the team measured, what they changed, and how other engineering teams can apply the approach → https://t.co/fs0nAEdTtX

items.title: Cohere Chief AI Officer @joellepineau argues the world's most powerful AI models are often a waste o...
items.content:
Cohere Chief AI Officer @joellepineau argues the world's most powerful AI models are often a waste of money for businesses:

"Cohere was founded in 2019. Aidan Gomez, our CEO, one of the authors on the Transformer paper."

"They made choices of focusing on enterprise versus consumer, which gives the work less visibility. And headquartered in Canada, which has some impact on the early funding trajectory."

"We try not to over-optimize on the indexes and to produce models that are high value for money and yet within that margin of the frontier."

"A lot of our customers actually don't want to run frontier models. They're way too expensive. They're not necessary for the workloads they have."

"We're model agnostic in our platform, so we offer a mix depending on security, cost-effectiveness, and capabilities. We pick our lanes where we really bring value."
@cohere

"In a shorter timeline scenario, OpenAI and Anthropic will pull ahead of the other labs."

@MNX_fi

items.content:
Cohere Chief AI Officer @joellepineau argues Canadian PM Mark Carney's critics are wrong:

The US and China don't have a monopoly on frontier AI.

"I disagree very strongly with that premise, to the point that it's why I decided to join Cohere."

"Building for the frontier is a choice. There's enough circulation of talent between Cohere and the other frontier labs that the recipe is reasonably well known."

"The main blocker on compute is access to capital. And then it's talent, and we have a phenomenal pool of talent in Canada anchored in Mila, Vector, and others."

"It's hard work to build frontier models. Every day you've got to hustle to get access to the compute and make the right technical choices. You can't afford to take a wrong turn in your training strategy."
@cohere
items.author: @MTSlive

items.title: Epoch AI researcher @AlexBarry4 warns that banks, hospitals, and water systems may not be able to pa...
items.content:
Epoch AI researcher @AlexBarry4 warns that banks, hospitals, and water systems may not be able to patch their software fast enough to keep up with AI-powered cyberattacks:

"Over the next year, I feel comparatively pessimistic."

"Everyone knew we were building all of the internet on incredibly insecure software all the way down, and somehow we got away with it for a few decades."

"I'm relatively pessimistic that we’re going to be able to patch everything. Will every bank, every hospital, every local water supply company be able to patch all their software? I expect we’re in for a pretty rocky time."

"In the longer term, some people think software could have no bugs in it. I'm not sure I'm that optimistic, but it’s plausible. Even before then, a rocky road."
@EpochAIResearch

Yeah, the worst thing about X now is the AI replies. 

Worse, I used to do lots of short replies to people and now I don't because I think I'm starting to sound like AI.

Well, I still appreciate human replies. Or, at least, the AI ones that add value.

items.title: Epoch AI researcher @AlexBarry4 warns that ignoring software updates is becoming far more dangerous ...
items.content:
Epoch AI researcher @AlexBarry4 warns that ignoring software updates is becoming far more dangerous as AI can develop exploits in as little as 12 hours:

"There's a little pop-up saying restart to update now, and you're always like, ignore, tell me later."

"That can leave you vulnerable, and we expect that's going to be more and more relevant, because AI can do this very quickly."

"Part of why this was less extreme when humans had to do the exploit development was, if it takes a human a week or two to craft the exploit, that’s quite a lot of time for people to update their software."

"We gave GLM 5.3 up to two days. In the fastest cases it was more like 12 hours. I wouldn’t be surprised if people could get that substantially faster."

"Keep your software up to date. If you have software you can predict will get out of date because you rarely use it or it’s annoying to update, think twice about whether you need it. Or boot up your own agent and be like, hey Claude, please update all my software."
@EpochAIResearch

items.content:
How do the views of AI industry experts differ from those of other experts?

Earlier this month, we asked participants in the Longitudinal Expert AI Panel about their forecasts and views on a number of policy proposals to mitigate risk from AI. Our expert panelists include:

• AI industry professionals
• Top computer scientists
• Leading economists
• Policy experts

We compared the policy forecasts and preferences from AI industry professionals to those from experts from other groups. Broadly speaking, AI industry professionals hold similar risk beliefs to other experts, and have similar policy beliefs and preferences, too.

More details in the thread ⬇️

items.content:
Hyperflow H3 lands at #5 on AA-Video-I2V v2.1 and #3 on AA-Video-Editing v1.1, at under half the price of Dreamina Seedance 2.5 on both

Hyperflow H3 is Video Rebirth's 8-step LoRA for MiniMax H3, released in September 2026 with open weights, and now supports Image to Video and Video Editing.

Hyperflow H3 places #5 on AA-Video-I2V v2.1. In our testing, it does best on Live-Action Film, where only Dreamina Seedance 2.5 ranks higher, and on Multi-Scene & Narrative, where only Utopai X scores higher. On AA-Video-Editing v1.1, it ranks #3, ahead of MiniMax H3 (768p), the model it builds on.

Hyperflow H3 is priced at $9.00 per minute for Image to Video and $18.00 per minute for Video Editing, both at 1088p on Video Rebirth's API.

Congratulations to @video_rebirth on the release!

See below for our analysis of Hyperflow H3 in Image to Video and Video Editing 🧵
items.author: @ArtificialAnlys
items.summary: Artificial Analysis reports benchmark results for Hyperflow H3, an 8-step LoRA by Video Rebirth built on MiniMax H3 with open weights (released September 2026). The model ranks #5 on the AA-Video-I2I v2.1 image-to-video leaderboard and #3 on AA-Video-Editing v1.1, outperforming its base MiniMax H3 (768p) on editing. It excels in Live-Action Film and Multi-Scene & Narrative categories, and is priced at $9.00/minute for image-to-video and $18.00/minute for video editing at 1088p — under half the cost of Dreamina Seedance 2.5.

items.title: LLMs are increasingly deployed in task-specific enterprise applications, such as customer support, d...
items.content:
LLMs are increasingly deployed in task-specific enterprise applications, such as customer support, document question answering, and code generation. However, current models tend to answer nearly any prompt regardless of relevance, leaving them vulnerable to distraction, off-brand behavior, and adversarial prompt injections. Unlike safety alignment, which focuses on suppressing a narrow band of toxic or dangerous outputs, restricting models to a bounded operational domain requires rejecting a broad universe of irrelevant queries while preserving high-quality answers for legitimate requests.

The article evaluates how effectively language models can be restricted to specific operational domains—a task defined as scoping—without degrading performance on authorized tasks. It systematically benchmarks five technical intervention strategies against standard system prompting across multiple model architectures and task domains.

items.title: Real-time translation must balance speed against accuracy: translating early reduces delay, but inco...
items.content:
Real-time translation must balance speed against accuracy: translating early reduces delay, but incomplete speech can leave the system without context needed for a reliable translation. In standard translation systems, this balance is often controlled with fixed timing rules that cannot respond to how uncertain a particular phrase is. The article addresses whether a system can be trained to decide more selectively what it is safe to translate as input arrives.

The article introduces a training method for cascaded translation, in which recognized speech is passed to a separate translation model. It creates “stable” partial translations by comparing translations of progressively longer source prefixes with the translation of the complete sentence, and retaining only the target text that agrees with the full-sentence translation. The researchers used these examples to fine-tune Qwen3-8B, then tested the system translating from English into German, Japanese, and Chinese. Evaluation covered three test sets and compared quality and delay under several ways of controlling when output is committed.

items.title: In summary, LEAP's AI industry experts, taken as a group, are close to the all-expert median on both...
items.content:
In summary, LEAP's AI industry experts, taken as a group, are close to the all-expert median on both absolute risk and the effect of the policies we asked them about. Where a single expert category diverges from that median, it is most often the policy experts.

There are a few important caveats to these findings:

• The expert group sample sizes are small (AI expert n = 38), and these differences are vulnerable to noise (see below for charts with bootstrapped 95% CIs)
• Comparing group medians obscures differences within groups, which can sometimes be large. For example, a quarter of respondents in our AI industry sample had a baseline risk forecast of 5% or higher, much higher than the median 2%.
• We can't claim that our AI industry subsample is representative of AI industry experts more generally. For more detail on our sampling, see the LEAP launch paper: https://t.co/WEKVlJG0po

To learn more about our findings from the LEAP policy wave, see below:

The US government...
items.content:
Valarian CBO @neemustafa explains why Europe wants independence from American AI:

The US government can compel American tech companies to hand over data stored anywhere in the world.

"The European Union has 450 million people. It's larger than the United States. But when people think about technology in the EU, it doesn't make sense proportionally relative to the population, relative to the wealth."

"Many years ago the US passed the CLOUD Act, which allows the American government to compel any American company that stores data anywhere in the world to share it. The hyperscalers are all American. The frontier labs are all American."

"I'm a proud American. It's not anti-American. People should have choice.”

"If you can't choose it, you don't have sovereignty. In the same way, in democracy, if you can't vote, you don't have sovereignty."
@Valarian

items.content:
.@pitdesi explains why AI is transforming Silicon Valley but barely showing up in the wider economy, and why 2027 could change everything:

"For people like us in the center, AI is everything. We're using it 100 times a day. And what we are experiencing has not shown up in national numbers yet."

"Coding is a great use case, and technologists use it first. Math is verifiable. Law is writing, and AI was fairly decent at writing already in 2023. Word cells were f*cked already."

"But then models like o3 come out and all of a sudden it's not making math errors. Remember how many Rs in strawberry? All that shit is gone."

"Now we are very close to solving accounting. Accounting is the base of so many things, and we have a shortage of accountants. More and more companies are getting AI pilled. I think 2027 is a big year."
@btv_vc

items.content:
𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗿 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸 𝗿𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

We asked participants how their risk forecasts would change, conditional on the independent implementation of the following policies:

• Federal preemption of state AI laws
• A "pacing the frontier" policy to slow frontier AI development (both US-only and US–China versions)
• Pre-release authorization for frontier models (both US and international versions)
• Strict liability (US statute treating frontier model training and deployment as an abnormally dangerous activity, and making developers liable for harms their models cause without the injured party having to prove the developer was careless or the model defective)
• Policy bundle incorporating a US–China slowdown, international pre-release authorization, and strict liability

Generally, AI industry experts' risk reduction expectations are similar to the expert group median.

Federal preemption is a notable exception. AI industry experts forecast this to increase risk by 25%, while the group median expects 50%. Here, AI industry experts are similar to policy experts (who also expect a 25% increase in risk), and very different from computer scientists (who expect a 100% increase in risk).

What you see happening in France is essentially what will happen throughout the whole of Western and Southern Europe at some point

Europe regulated away all new and existing businesses so they with the money and the talent moved elsewhere (like US and Asia)

When money flees a continent, the businesses, then the people and the government run out of money

Meanwhile cost of living keeps growing → people get poorer and → people need more government welfare → meaning the government has to borrow more money to pay for that → borrowing for worse and worse rates → which pushes down the Euro → meaning less spending power for its people → making Europeans even poorer

items.title: Rocker CEO @alexvogenthaler explains why two-thirds of companies are seeing no bottom-line impact fr...
items.content:
Rocker CEO @alexvogenthaler explains why two-thirds of companies are seeing no bottom-line impact from AI, even as their employees become dramatically faster:

"The latest study from McKinsey showed that two-thirds of companies are not seeing impact from AI adoption, yet we've supercharged all of these individuals. How can that possibly be."

"You can have a company full of superfast individuals and not have it translate into the fastest company, because individuals mostly don’t accomplish things in isolation."

"She's gonna deliver that feature three times as fast as before. Is it gonna translate into impact for the company? It might not, because actually we didn't build the thing that the market needed."

"Individuals being able to move super fast is a necessary condition for companies speeding up, but it's not a sufficient condition for the company as a whole to be able to speed up."

Valarian CBO @neemustafa reveals the hidden problem with Perplexity Computer:

It was making API calls to outside vendors that enterprise customers didn't even know about.

"NEA led the Series A in Perplexity, so I was actually the one who made this introduction to the Valarian guys. Within a week or two, the Valarian guys are saying, these guys are really serious."

"When Perplexity was running Computer, there were many network calls, API calls, still being made that customers weren't aware of. For a lot of regulated enterprises, they just can’t have that."

"ACRA adds policy. You have Perplexity's amazing Computer engine for agents, and the Valarian policy engine controls what can go in, what can go out, what permissions, what security postures."
@Valarian

items.title: Fine-tuning 3D vision models for specialized tasks often requires real-world 3D data that is costly,...
items.content:
Fine-tuning 3D vision models for specialized tasks often requires real-world 3D data that is costly, difficult, or privacy-sensitive to collect. Standard parameter-efficient approaches can also struggle to adapt reliably: small updates may miss important changes, while larger ones may overfit. The article asks whether recurring types of 3D variation—texture, geometry, camera motion, and lighting—can be represented by reusable, separate update directions that make fine-tuning both more efficient and more accurate.

The article develops a method using the VGGT 3D foundation model. The researchers generated synthetic scenes in which one visual property varied substantially while the others were kept relatively stable. They fine-tuned separate low-rank adapters on multiple datasets for each property, then combined the resulting model updates to identify the directions shared across datasets. These property-specific directions were largely distinct from one another and were assembled into a compact basis for adapting the model to new tasks. Tests covered face reconstruction from tightly spaced views, clothed-human reconstruction, and transparent-object reconstruction, using both synthetic and real-world evaluation data.

items.title: Scaling modern vision systems through end-to-end retraining imposes severe financial and computation...
items.content:
Scaling modern vision systems through end-to-end retraining imposes severe financial and computational costs. While model merging can synthesize knowledge from pre-trained checkpoints without costly retraining, current weight-averaging techniques require models to share identical architectures and parameter shapes. Consequently, practitioners cannot directly combine the complementary benefits of global Vision Transformers and linear-scaling state-space models. The article evaluates a framework designed to bridge these architecturally incompatible families by mapping their parameters to a common representation and fusing them geometrically.

To address this challenge, the article introduces Riemannian–Lorentz Parameter Fusion. Instead of forcing parameters into a single network, the approach maintains both architectures side by side in a two-branch hybrid system. Parameters are aligned by functional role—specifically grouping patch embeddings, sequence-mixing blocks, feed-forward layers, and normalization layers—and projected into a shared latent space using singular-value decomposition. The method then computes a regularized geometric average in curved hyperbolic space using the Lorentz model, decodes the values back to the separate branches, and applies a learned gating mechanism to dynamically blend the predictions for each input image. Experiments were conducted across CIFAR-10, Oxford-IIIT Pet, and ImageNet-1K using ViT-Tiny and PlainMamba-L1 parent models.

items.title: As LLMs are deployed across mission-critical systems, debugging their operational failures has becom...
items.content:
As LLMs are deployed across mission-critical systems, debugging their operational failures has become an urgent technical and business necessity. Most current evaluation workflows treat models as black boxes by examining only inputs and final answers. While this behavioral analysis identifies that a failure happened, it cannot explain why it occurred. Meanwhile, standard interpretability techniques have historically been confined to simplified test environments and short prompt templates. They struggle to scale to the complex tasks and long input contexts characteristic of real-world deployments.

The article evaluates whether interpretability tools can provide actionable diagnostic value for real-world language model failures. Specifically, the authors demonstrate how examining a model's internal decision states across layers can pinpoint the root causes of errors, verify genuine gains from model scaling, and track how models learn across training stages.

items.title: I love books. Especially high-quality textbooks written by an author who has both mastered and loved...
items.content:
I love books. Especially high-quality textbooks written by an author who has both mastered and loved their craft.

What makes me sad about textbooks, especially tech textbooks, is that they become outdated. Some faster than others.

Some authors keep their books up to date by releasing new editions, but some wonderful books don't get this chance.

I once bought the book Programming Collective Intelligence by Toby Segaran, and it was the book that made me fall in love with machine learning and data science.

Many years later, I even wanted to contact Toby Segaran and offer to revise his book, update the outdated parts, and replace some datasets and algorithms with more powerful alternatives. Unfortunately, Toby Segaran passed away before I got this idea, and now his absolutely must-read book, published in 2007 and now outdated, cannot have a new life because copyright law doesn't allow anyone to adopt this book and give it a new life.

But when a book is published under one of the Creative Commons licenses, such as CC-BY or CC-BY-SA, or under the GNU FDL license, anyone can take a book the author is no longer maintaining and start maintaining it.

So, I thought that while I cannot save Toby's book, I can save some other great books. I started with A Byte of Python by Swaroop C.H. The book was published in 2004 and has never been updated since.

I updated the installation instructions and first steps, changed the Unix-style examples and code blocks to reflect updated APIs and conventions, fixed all the facts that are no longer true in 2026 and broken links, and corrected plenty of small errors and typos here and there.

Now A Byte of Python is great again and is available in two versions on ChapterPal: the author's original version and my upgraded/corrected version. The user can choose which version they prefer to read.

So far, I've upgraded/corrected this way two books. Eventually, all ChapterPal books with permissive licenses will be regularly updated.

Read A Byte of Python on ChapterPal: https://t.co/9IaZjgCpJ4

Where Hyperflow H3 is strongest in Image to Video: only Utopai X scores higher on Multi-Scene & Narrative, and Spatio-Temporal Consistency is where it improves most on MiniMax H3 (768p)

Capabilities are the model skills a prompt is written to test. In AA-Video-I2V v2.1, every prompt pairs a starting image with a text prompt written for that image.

➤ Spatio-Temporal Consistency covers spatial coherence, time lapses, occlusion and re-entry, and single-shot stories.

➤ Human Anatomy, where Hyperflow H3 trails the leaders most, covers gait and locomotion, fine motor movement, facial expression, acrobatic motion, object grasping, and human interaction.

items.title: Advanced technologies can reshape economies and everyday life, but their gains may accrue mainly to ...
items.content:
Advanced technologies can reshape economies and everyday life, but their gains may accrue mainly to the people and organizations that control them. The article asks who should benefit when technologies with society-wide effects—especially advanced AI—are developed in a world marked by poverty, unequal opportunity, and uneven access to technology. Its central conclusion is that everyone has a moral claim to receive material benefit from transformative technologies, even though inventors and investors may also deserve returns for their contributions.

The article develops this case through five complementary moral arguments: human rights, the duty to prevent avoidable harm and wasted potential, fairness in the face of unequal circumstances of birth, reciprocity for humanity’s shared stock of knowledge and contributions, and justice within the global economic system. This is a philosophical analysis, not an empirical test of a particular technology or distribution policy. It draws on ethical theories, human-rights principles, historical examples, and research on global inequality, technological development, and economic institutions. The authors examine objections as well as supporting arguments, and emphasize that no single argument settles every case.

But I see them all over Portugal (and ...
items.content:
Today I want to show you something I never saw anywhere else

But I see them all over Portugal (and apparently Spain too)

They're giant warehouses in the middle of nowhere with big red signs saying MEGA CHINA, HIPER CHINA, MAXI CHINA, or even GRANDE CHINA

They're shops by Chinese immigrants from a single place in China, the Zheijang province (where Alibaba is also from)

The story is that they came to Southern Europe in the 1990s and 2000s and built these shops

They started as small shops but then during the financial crisis in 2008, there was suddenly lots of super cheap warehouses from bankrupt Portuguese companies so they took them over and turned their tiny shops into massive stores

Now they're anything but small, they're MEGA CHINA

It's a tight family run network with a few distribution hubs that supply the shops and in the hubs then get supplied by container ships from China. Way more advanced than I first thought

China is everywhere, even in the middle of nowhere in Portugal!

(Part 2 in reply)

Some people say they don't believe these numbers

So calculate it for yourself:

~115 deaths ÷ ~35M high speed train trips
=
1 in 300,000 is the statistical odds of death per trip in a Spanish high speed train this year

You can then argue "why do you cherry pick only this year", well because it happened this year! It's new information and you have 2 highly similar fatal accidents happening in one year meaning the probability that's random is almost zero

It's like saying after the 737 Max crashes that killed 346 people in 2018/2019

"That's just a random statistical oddity, I'll board the next one immediately"

Of course you wouldn't

What you'd do is board none at all until it's fully investigated why they crashed and the cause is solved, like the FAA did exactly by grounding them

To all the Spanish nationalist keyboard warriors attacking me instead of their government:

Pivot your energy to prosecuting the people responsible for killing 100+ innocent people this year instead of shooting the messenger!

items.title:
@itsanotherjon No it wouldn't 

"The “35M trips” counts passenger journeys (one person, one ride), n...
items.content:
@itsanotherjon No it wouldn't 

"The “35M trips” counts passenger journeys (one person, one ride), not trains, and that’s why the calculation works.

So 115 deaths ÷ ~35M passenger journeys is the chance that any one person’s ride ends with them dead. That’s already “the odds of dying yourself.”

What they describe is a different number: the odds of being on a train that has a fatal crash. Both are useful, and they connect:

Odds of being on a fatal-crash train: about 400 people were on the two Adamuz trains and 544 on the two Urda trains, so ~944 of ~35M high-speed/long-distance journeys ≈ 1 in 37,000
Odds of dying if you’re on one: 115 of ~944 ≈ 12%
Combined: 1/37,000 × 12% ≈ 1 in 300,000, the same number as before

The ~1 in 300,000 per-trip figure stands. It’s even slightly pessimistic for passengers, because a few of the dead were crew, including the Alvia driver and a crew member at Urda."
